cor-birkhoff-convex-combination.title: Birkhoff’s Theorem with a Count
cor-birkhoff-convex-combination.html: Let n≥1. Every M∈Ωn is a convex combination of at most (n−1)2+1 permutation matrices.

cor-doubly-stochastic-positive-diagonal.title: A Positive Diagonal
cor-doubly-stochastic-positive-diagonal.html: Let M∈Ωn. Then there is a permutation σ∈Sn with mσ(j)j>0 for every j=1,…,n.

cor-left-perron-vector.title: The Left Perron Vector
cor-left-perron-vector.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be non-negative and irreducible, with ρ=ρ(A) and v>0 as in @thm-perron-frobenius. Then:

  1. A⊤ is non-negative and irreducible, and ρ(A⊤)=ρ;
  2. there is w>0 with w⊤A=ρw⊤, and every non-negative left eigenvector of A is a positive multiple of w;
  3. w⊤v>0, so w can be scaled to make w⊤v=1.

cor-leontief-productive.title: Productive Economies
cor-leontief-productive.html:
Let C∈Mn(R) with C≥0. The following are equivalent.

  1. For every d≥0 there is x≥0 with (I−C)x=d.
  2. There is x≥0 with x−Cx>0: some plan leaves a surplus of every good.
  3. ρ(C)<1.
  4. I−C is invertible and (I−C)−1≥0.
  5. Every leading principal minor of I−C is positive.

When they hold, the solution in (i) is unique, and (I−C)−1=I+C+C2+⋯. They hold in particular when every column sum of C is less than 1.

cor-primitive-iff-aperiodic.title: Primitivity from Walks
cor-primitive-iff-aperiodic.html: Let A∈Mn(R), A≥0, be irreducible and not the 1×1 zero matrix. Then A is primitive if and only if its period is 1. In particular, an irreducible A≥0 with at least one positive diagonal entry is primitive.

cor-row-sum-bounds-rho.title: Row and Column Sums Bound the Spectral Radius
cor-row-sum-bounds-rho.title_html: Row and Column Sums Bound the Spectral Radius
cor-row-sum-bounds-rho.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) with A≥0.

  1. miniri≤ρ(A)≤maxiri and minjcj≤ρ(A)≤maxjcj.
  2. If A is irreducible, then ρ(A)=miniri if and only if ρ(A)=maxiri, if and only if all the row sums are equal. The same holds for the column sums.

cor-symmetric-m-matrix-positive-definite.title: Symmetric M-Matrices Are Positive Definite
cor-symmetric-m-matrix-positive-definite.html: A symmetric Z-matrix A∈Mn(R) is a non-singular M-matrix if and only if A≻0.

def-absorbing-chain.title: Absorbing Chain
def-absorbing-chain.html: A stochastic matrix A∈Mn(R) is absorbing if it has at least one absorbing state, and from every state some absorbing state can be reached: for every j there are an absorbing state i and an m≥0 with (Am)ij>0. The states that are not absorbing are called transient.

def-collatz-wielandt-functions.title: Collatz–Wielandt Functions
def-collatz-wielandt-functions.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) with A≥0.

  1. For x≥0 with x≠0, the lower Collatz–Wielandt function is r―A(x):=min{(Ax)ixi:1≤i≤n, xi>0}.
  2. For x>0, the upper Collatz–Wielandt function is r―A(x):=max{(Ax)ixi:1≤i≤n}.

def-directed-graph-of-matrix.title: Directed Graph of a Matrix; Walks and Paths
def-directed-graph-of-matrix.title_html: Directed Graph of a Matrix; Walks and Paths
def-directed-graph-of-matrix.html:
Let n≥1 and A=(aij)∈Mn(F).

  1. The directed graph G(A) of A has vertices 1,2,…,n, and an edge from j to i, written j→i, for each pair (i,j) with aij≠0. An edge j→j, from a non-zero diagonal entry, is a loop.
  2. A walk of length k≥0 from j to i is a list of vertices j=i0,i1,…,ik=i such that it−1→it is an edge for every t=1,…,k.
  3. A path is a walk whose vertices i0,…,ik are distinct.

def-entrywise-order.title: Entrywise Order; Non-negative and Positive Matrices
def-entrywise-order.title_html: Entrywise Order; Non-negative and Positive Matrices
def-entrywise-order.html:
Let A=(aij) and B=(bij) be real m×n matrices.

  1. A≥B means aij≥bij for every i,j, and A>B means aij>bij for every i,j. We write B≤A and B<A for the same statements.
  2. A is non-negative if A≥0, and positive if A>0, where 0 is the zero matrix of the same shape.
  3. For a complex m×n matrix M=(mij), the entrywise absolute value is the real matrix |M|:=(|mij|).

Vectors are the case n=1, so x≥0, x>0 and |x|=(|x1|,…,|xn|) have the same meaning as in Chapter 17 §05.

def-google-matrix.title: Google Matrix, PageRank Vector
def-google-matrix.html: Let P∈Mn(R) be the link matrix of a web with n≥1 pages, and let 0<α<1. The matrix G=αP+1−αnJ is called the Google matrix in the literature, with damping factor α. A PageRank vector of the web is a probability vector 𝛑π∈Rn with 𝛑𝛑Gπ=π. Page i is ranked above page k when πi>πk.

def-irreducible.title: Irreducible Matrix
def-irreducible.html:
Let A∈Mn(F).

  1. For n≥2, A is reducible if there are a permutation matrix P and an integer k with 1≤k≤n−1 such that P⊤AP=(BC0D),B∈Mk(F), D∈Mn−k(F), with 0 the (n−k)×k zero matrix. It is irreducible if it is not reducible.
  2. For n=1, every matrix (a)∈M1(F) is irreducible, including (0).

def-link-matrix.title: Link Matrix
def-link-matrix.html:
Let a web have pages 1,…,n, with n≥1, and out-degrees d1,…,dn. Its link matrix is the n×n matrix P whose column j is:

  1. if dj≥1: the vector with entry 1/dj in each position i such that page j links to page i, and 0 elsewhere;
  2. if dj=0 (page j is dangling): the vector 1n1.

def-m-matrix.title: M-Matrix
def-m-matrix.html: A matrix A∈Mn(R), n≥1, is an M-matrix if it can be written as A=sI−Bwith s∈R, B∈Mn(R), B≥0 and s≥ρ(B). An M-matrix that is invertible is a non-singular M-matrix.

def-period.title: Period
def-period.html: Let A∈Mn(R), A≥0, be irreducible and not the 1×1 zero matrix. The period of A is the greatest common divisor of the lengths of all closed walks in A.

def-perron-root-and-vectors.title: Perron Root, Perron Vectors
def-perron-root-and-vectors.html: This definition extends @def-perron-vector from positive matrices to irreducible ones. Let A∈Mn(R) be non-negative and irreducible. Its Perron root is ρ(A). Its (right) Perron vector is the unique v>0 with Av=ρ(A)v and 1⊤v=1. Its left Perron vector is the unique w>0 with w⊤A=ρ(A)w⊤ and w⊤v=1.

def-perron-vector.title: Perron Root, Perron Vector
def-perron-vector.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be positive. The number ρ(A) is the Perron root of A. The Perron vector of A is the unique v>0 with Av=ρ(A)v and v1+⋯+vn=1. The left Perron vector of A is the unique w>0 with w⊤A=ρ(A)w⊤ and w⊤v=1, where v is the Perron vector.

def-primitive.title: Primitive Matrix
def-primitive.html: A matrix A∈Mn(R), n≥1, with A≥0 is primitive if Ak>0 for some integer k≥1, that is, if every entry of some power of A is strictly positive.

def-strongly-connected.title: Strongly Connected
def-strongly-connected.html: Let A∈Mn(F). The graph G(A) is strongly connected if, for every ordered pair (j,i) of vertices, there is a walk from j to i.

def-z-matrix.title: Z-Matrix
def-z-matrix.html: A matrix A=(aij)∈Mn(R), n≥1, is a Z-matrix if aij≤0 for every pair i≠j.

exm-birkhoff-peeling.html: Write M=18(4220130430410323) as a convex combination of permutation matrices.

exm-cycle-power.title: The cycle, by one power
exm-cycle-power.html: For the cycle C=(001100010), compute (I+C)2, and compare with the powers Ck.

exm-cyclic-permutation.title: The Cyclic Permutation
exm-cyclic-permutation.html: Let n≥2 and let σ∈Sn send j↦j+1 for j<n and n↦1. Its permutation matrix P=Pσ (@def-permutation-matrix) has columns e2,e3,…,en,e1. Show that P is irreducible with period n, find its peripheral eigenvalues, and show that Pm does not converge.

exm-estimate-rho-test-vectors.title: Trapping the spectral radius
exm-estimate-rho-test-vectors.html: For the matrix A of @exm-row-column-sum-bounds, compute the brackets [r―A(x),r―A(x)] for x=1,A1,A21,A31,A41. Hence give ρ(A) to two decimal places, and check the answer against the characteristic polynomial.

exm-gamblers-ruin.title: Gambler’s Ruin
exm-gamblers-ruin.html: A gambler holds 1, 2 or 3 coins and bets one coin at a time on a fair toss, winning or losing a coin with probability 12 each. Play stops when the gambler holds 0 coins (ruin) or 4 coins (target). Find the fundamental matrix, the expected length of play, and the probability of reaching the target, from each starting fortune.

exm-leontief-three-sectors.title: Three Sectors
exm-leontief-three-sectors.html: An economy has three sectors, agriculture, manufacturing and services, with consumption matrix C=15(111201021). Show that it is productive, find ρ(C) exactly, compute the Leontief inverse, and find the production plan meeting the demand d=(12,6,6).

exm-perron-conclusions-lost.title_html: Three non-negative matrices that break Perron’s theorem

exm-spectral-radius-monotone.html: Let A=(1210) and B=(1211). Compute both spectral radii and compare with @prp-spectral-radius-monotone.

exr-birkhoff-a1.title: A1
exr-birkhoff-a1.html:
1. State Birkhoff’s theorem in both forms.
  2. Name the results of Chapter 17 that the proof of @thm-birkhoff uses, and say what each contributes.
  3. What upper bound does Step 1 of the proof give for the number of non-zero entries of a vertex of Ω4? How many does a vertex actually have?
  4. True or false: every matrix in Ωn with at most 2n−1 non-zero entries is a permutation matrix. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: the product of two doubly stochastic matrices is doubly stochastic. Justify your answer.
  6. True or false: every M∈Ω3 is a convex combination of at most five permutation matrices. Justify your answer.

exr-birkhoff-b2.title: B2: Peeling a 3 × 3 matrix

exr-birkhoff-b3.title: B3: Schur’s theorem by averaging
exr-birkhoff-b3.html:
Let A=(4221).

  1. Find 𝛌λ(A) and an orthogonal U with 𝛌A=Udiag(λ(A))U⊤.
  2. Compute S=(uij2) and check that 𝛌d(A)=Sλ(A).

exr-birkhoff-c1.title: C1: Five permutation matrices can be needed
exr-birkhoff-c1.title_html: C1: Five permutation matrices can be needed
exr-birkhoff-c1.html:
Let P be the permutation matrix of the 3-cycle 1↦2↦3↦1, and let T12,T13,T23 be those of the transpositions (1 2),(1 3),(2 3). The six permutation matrices of size 3 are I,P,P2 (the even ones) and T12,T13,T23 (the odd ones).

  1. Show that each of the nine positions (i,j) holds a 1 in exactly one even and exactly one odd permutation matrix, and that each even and each odd permutation matrix share exactly one position of a 1.
  2. Deduce that if ∑σcσPσ=0 for real numbers cσ, then cσ=c for the even σ and cσ=−c for the odd σ, for some c∈R.
  3. Let M=115(I+2P+3P2+4T12+5T13). Show that every way of writing M as a convex combination of permutation matrices uses at least five of them with positive weight.

Hint: in (a), a permutation of {1,2,3} is determined by where it sends any two points.

exr-birkhoff-c2.title: C2: Integer matrices with equal line sums
exr-birkhoff-c2.title_html: C2: Integer matrices with equal line sums

Let k≥1, and let N∈Mn(R) have non-negative integer entries, with every row and every column adding up to k.

  2. Carry this out for N=(210012111).

Hint: apply @cor-doubly-stochastic-positive-diagonal to 1kN.

exr-birkhoff-c3.title: C3: The dimension, and a matrix that is not unistochastic
exr-birkhoff-c3.title_html: C3: The dimension, and a matrix that is not unistochastic

  2. Show that M=12(110011101) is doubly stochastic but is not of the form (|uij|2) for any unitary U∈M3(C).

Hint for (b): two columns of U must be orthogonal; look at which rows both can be non-zero in.

exr-irreducibility-and-graphs-c3.title: C3: Irreducibility as growth of supports
exr-irreducibility-and-graphs-c3.title_html: C3: Irreducibility as growth of supports

Let n≥2 and A∈Mn(R) with A≥0. For x≥0, call {i:xi>0} the support of x.

  1. Prove that the support of (I+A)x is the support S of x together with every vertex i for which there is an edge j→i with j∈S.
  2. Prove that A is irreducible if and only if, for every x≥0 with at least one zero entry and at least one positive entry, (I+A)x has more positive entries than x.
  3. Deduce, without using walks, that (I+A)n−1x>0 for every non-zero x≥0 when A is irreducible, and hence that (I+A)n−1>0.

Hint for (b): use @lem-reducible-closed-set.

exr-m-matrices-a1.title: A1
exr-m-matrices-a1.html:
1. Define a Z-matrix and a non-singular M-matrix.
  2. True or false: every Z-matrix with positive diagonal entries is a non-singular M-matrix. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: every principal submatrix of a non-singular M-matrix is a non-singular M-matrix. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A is invertible and A−1≥0, then A is an M-matrix. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: the inverse of a non-singular M-matrix has every entry positive. Justify your answer.
  6. Name a vector x>0 with Knx>0, and explain why x=1 does not work when n≥3.

exr-m-matrices-b1.title: B1: Which are non-singular M-matrices?
exr-m-matrices-b1.html:
Determine which of the following are non-singular M-matrices. Justify your answer.

  1. (3−1−1−13−1−1−13)
  2. (1−10−12−10−11)
  3. (2−3−12)
  4. (2112)
  5. (1−2001−2−201)

exr-m-matrices-b2.title: B2: A string with a free end
exr-m-matrices-b2.title_html: B2: A string with a free end
exr-m-matrices-b2.html:
Let A=(2−10−12−10−11).

  1. Show that A1 is not positive, and find x>0 with Ax>0.
  2. Compute the leading principal minors of A, and check that they agree with (a).
  3. Compute A−1 and check that A−1≥0. Hence solve Au=e3, and say why the answer had to be non-negative.

Hint: try an increasing x whose increments decrease.

exr-m-matrices-b3.title: B3: A two-sector economy
exr-m-matrices-b3.html:
Let C=(1/52/53/101/10).

  1. Show that the economy with consumption matrix C is productive.
  2. Compute the Leontief inverse (I−C)−1.
  3. Find the production plan meeting the demand d=(30,60), and check it.
  4. Find ρ(C) exactly.

exr-m-matrices-c1.title: C1: Raising the diagonal
exr-m-matrices-c1.html:
1. Let A be a non-singular M-matrix and M a Z-matrix of the same size with M≥A entrywise. Prove that M is a non-singular M-matrix and that 0≤M−1≤A−1.
  2. Deduce that for every diagonal D≥0, Kn+D is a non-singular M-matrix with (Kn+D)−1≤Kn−1. Check this for n=2 and D=diag(1,0).

Hint: for the inequality, factor A−1−M−1.

exr-m-matrices-c2.title: C2: The singular case
exr-m-matrices-c2.html:
1. Show that the Z-matrix Z=(0−10−1) has non-negative leading principal minors but is not an M-matrix.
  2. Let A be an M-matrix. Prove that A+εI is a non-singular M-matrix for every real ε>0.
  3. Deduce that every principal minor of an M-matrix is non-negative.
  4. Check (c) for (1−1−11), and explain why (a) does not contradict the stated converse in the remark after @thm-m-matrix-characterizations.

exr-m-matrices-c3.title: C3: Non-negative dynamics
exr-m-matrices-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be a Z-matrix, written as A=sI−B with B≥0.

  1. Prove that e−tA≥0 for every real t≥0.
  2. Suppose A is a non-singular M-matrix, and let x be the solution of x′=−Ax with x(0)=x0≥0. Prove that x(t)≥0 for every t≥0 and that x(t)→0 as t→∞.

Hint: split −tA into two commuting matrices.

exr-markov-chains-a1.title: A1
exr-markov-chains-a1.html:
1. State the long-run theorem @thm-markov-limit-primitive, and name the three hypotheses of @thm-markov-limit-diagonalizable that it no longer needs.
  2. True or false: every irreducible stochastic matrix has exactly one steady state. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: for every irreducible stochastic matrix, Am converges. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if a stochastic matrix has two different steady states, it has infinitely many. Justify your answer.
  5. In an absorbing chain, what do the column sums of the fundamental matrix measure, and why do the columns of RN sum to 1?

exr-markov-chains-b1.title: B1: When does the long-run theorem apply?
exr-markov-chains-b1.title_html: B1: When does the long-run theorem apply?
exr-markov-chains-b1.html:
For each stochastic matrix, determine whether @thm-markov-limit-primitive applies. Justify your answer, and when it applies, find the limit of Am.

  1. (001/2100011/2).
  2. (001100010).
  3. (1/201/21).

exr-markov-chains-b2.title: B2: A three-state chain
exr-markov-chains-b2.html:
Let A=(1/21/401/21/21/201/41/2).

  1. Show that A is stochastic and that A2>0.
  2. Find the steady state, and hence limmAm and the long-run distribution of every chain with this transition matrix.

exr-markov-chains-b3.title: B3: An unfair game
exr-markov-chains-b3.html: A gambler holds 1 or 2 coins and wins each toss with probability 13, losing with probability 23. Play stops at 0 or 3 coins. Find the fundamental matrix, the expected length of play and the probability of reaching 3 coins from each starting fortune.

exr-markov-chains-c1.title: C1: The lazy chain
exr-markov-chains-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic and irreducible, with steady state v, and let M=12(I+A).

  1. Prove that M is stochastic and primitive, and that v is its unique steady state. Deduce that Mm→v1⊤.
  2. Let A be the walk of @exm-reflecting-walk. Show that M is the matrix of exercise B2, and that Mm=v1⊤+2−mF for every m≥1, where F=12(10−1000−101).

Hint: write M in terms of v1⊤ and F.

exr-markov-chains-c2.title: C2: The converse of the long-run theorem
exr-markov-chains-c2.title_html: C2: The converse of the long-run theorem
exr-markov-chains-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic.

  1. Prove that if Am→v1⊤ for some v>0, then A is primitive.
  2. Give a stochastic A with Am→v1⊤ for a probability vector v, but no power of A positive. Which entry of v is responsible?

exr-markov-chains-c3.title: C3: First-step analysis
exr-markov-chains-c3.html:
Let A be absorbing, with fundamental matrix N and 𝛕τ⊤=1⊤N.

  1. Prove that N=I+NQ, and deduce that τj=1+∑iqijτi for every transient j. Interpret this equation.
  2. Prove, by multiplying by R, that B=RN satisfies B=R+BQ, and interpret it.
  3. Use (a) to recompute the expected lengths of play (3,4,3) of @exm-gamblers-ruin without inverting a matrix.

exr-pagerank-a1.title: A1
exr-pagerank-a1.html:
1. Define the Google matrix of a web and its PageRank vector.
  2. Why is every entry of G positive, and which three conclusions does @thm-perron then give?
  3. True or false: with α=1, every web has exactly one PageRank vector. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: the page with the most incoming links always has the highest PageRank. Justify your answer.
  5. For α=0.85, what does @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues say about the eigenvalues of G other than 1? Can the bound be improved for every web?
  6. True or false: after 10 steps of xk+1=Gxk from any probability vector, 𝛑‖x10−π‖1≤2α10. Justify your answer.

exr-pagerank-b1.title: B1: A three-page web
exr-pagerank-b1.html: For the three-page web after @def-link-matrix (page 1 links to pages 2 and 3, page 2 to page 3, page 3 is dangling), with α=12, find the PageRank vector by solving the system of @thm-pagerank-vector (c). Hence rank the pages.

exr-pagerank-b2.title: B2: A cycle of three pages
exr-pagerank-b2.title_html: B2: A cycle of three pages
exr-pagerank-b2.html:
Three pages link in a cycle: 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1. Let 0<α<1.

  1. Write down P and show that pP(x)=x3−1.
  2. Use @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues to find the eigenvalues of G, and check your answer against trG.
  3. Find 𝛑π, and explain why the bound of @thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues is attained.

exr-pagerank-b3.title: B3: Personalized jumps
exr-pagerank-b3.html:
Let P∈Mn(R) be stochastic, 0<α<1, and let v be a probability vector with every vi>0. Put Gv=αP+(1−α)v1⊤: the surfer now jumps to page i with probability vi.

  1. Prove that Gv is stochastic and positive, and deduce that it has exactly one probability vector 𝛑π with 𝛑𝛑Gvπ=π, and that 𝛑π>0.
  2. Prove that 𝛑π is the unique solution of 𝛑(I−αP)π=(1−α)v.
  3. For two pages linking to each other, α=12 and v=(34,14), find 𝛑π.

exr-pagerank-c1.title: C1: PageRank as a sum over paths
exr-pagerank-c1.title_html: C1: PageRank as a sum over paths
exr-pagerank-c1.html:
Let P, α, G and 𝛑π be as in @thm-pagerank-vector.

  1. Prove that 𝛑π=1−αn∑k=0∞αkPk1.
  2. Deduce that πi≥1−αn for every i.
  3. Suppose no page is dangling and no page links to page i. Prove that πi=1−αn exactly.

Hint for (a): @thm-neumann-series with the 1-norm.

exr-pagerank-c2.title: C2: When the bound is attained
exr-pagerank-c2.title_html: C2: When the bound is attained
exr-pagerank-c2.html:
Let P∈Mn(R) be stochastic, 0<α<1, and G=αP+1−αnJ.

  1. Suppose P has two different steady states u≠w. Prove that G(u−w)=α(u−w), so that α is an eigenvalue of G.
  2. For the web of @exm-link-matrix-failures (b), find all eigenvalues of G, with multiplicity, and check your answer against (a).

exr-perron-frobenius-a1.title: A1
exr-perron-frobenius-a1.html:
1. State the Perron–Frobenius theorem for irreducible non-negative matrices.
  2. True or false: if A≥0, then ρ(A)>0. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: if A≥0 is irreducible, then every eigenvalue λ≠ρ(A) has |λ|<ρ(A). Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A≥0 and Ay=μy with y≥0, y≠0, then μ=ρ(A). Justify your answer.
  5. Which positive matrix does the proof of @thm-perron-frobenius apply @thm-perron to, and why not to A+εJ?

exr-perron-frobenius-b1.title: B1: Does the theorem apply?
exr-perron-frobenius-b1.html: For each matrix, determine whether @thm-perron-frobenius applies. Where it does, find ρ and a positive eigenvector; where it does not, say which hypothesis fails and whether the conclusion fails too. Justify your answers. (a) (0280)(b) (1203)(c) (010001100)(d) (0−110)

exr-perron-frobenius-b2.title: B2: Both Perron vectors
exr-perron-frobenius-b2.html: Let A=(010202101). Show that A is irreducible, and find its Perron root, its right Perron vector and its left Perron vector (@def-perron-root-and-vectors). Hence write down the matrix vw⊤ and check that it is idempotent.

exr-perron-frobenius-b3.title: B3: A reducible matrix, clause by clause
exr-perron-frobenius-b3.title_html: B3: A reducible matrix, clause by clause
exr-perron-frobenius-b3.html: Let A=(200130012). Show that A is reducible. Find ρ(A) and every non-negative eigenvector of A. Hence decide which of the four conclusions of @thm-perron-frobenius hold for A and which fail.

exr-perron-frobenius-c1.title: C1: A positive eigenvector always belongs to the spectral radius
exr-perron-frobenius-c1.title_html: C1: A positive eigenvector always belongs to the spectral radius
exr-perron-frobenius-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) with A≥0, not assumed irreducible.

  1. Prove that if Ax=μx with x>0, then μ=ρ(A).
  2. Deduce that if every row of A has the same sum s, then ρ(A)=s.
  3. Show by an example that (a) fails if x>0 is weakened to x≥0, x≠0.

Hint: apply @thm-nonnegative-rho-eigenvalue to A⊤.

exr-perron-frobenius-c2.title: C2: What the limit loses
exr-perron-frobenius-c2.html:
This exercise shows why the proof of @thm-perron-frobenius does not take the limit A+εJ→A.

  1. For ε>0, find the eigenvalues of I2+εJ. Show that ρ is simple for every ε>0, but not at ε=0.
  2. For ε>0, let Nε=(ε1+εεε), which is N+εJ for the nilpotent N of @exm-perron-conclusions-lost. Show that ρ(Nε)=ε+ε(1+ε) with eigenvector (1+ε, ε)>0, and find the limit of this eigenvector as ε→0+.
  3. Which conclusions of @thm-perron survive the limit in these two examples, and which do not? Explain in one sentence why this is to be expected.

exr-perron-frobenius-c3.title: C3: Uniqueness through the left Perron vector
exr-perron-frobenius-c3.title_html: C3: Uniqueness through the left Perron vector
exr-perron-frobenius-c3.html:
Let A≥0 be irreducible, with left Perron vector w (@def-perron-root-and-vectors, @cor-left-perron-vector).

  1. Using @thm-left-right-biorthogonal, give a second proof that if Ay=μy with y≥0, y≠0, then μ=ρ(A).
  2. Deduce that an irreducible stochastic matrix has exactly one steady state (@def-markov-chain), and that it is positive.

exr-positive-matrices-a1.title: A1
exr-positive-matrices-a1.html:
1. Define what it means for a real matrix to be non-negative and to be positive, and define |M| for a complex matrix M.
  2. State @thm-perron.
  3. True or false: a positive symmetric matrix is positive definite. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: a positive matrix has no negative eigenvalue. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if 0≤A≤B and A≠B, then ρ(A)<ρ(B). Justify your answer.
  6. In the proof of @thm-perron, which step uses compactness, and why is the quotient mini(Ax)i/xi not maximized directly?

exr-positive-matrices-b1.title: B1: A Perron vector by hand
exr-positive-matrices-b1.title_html: B1: A Perron vector by hand
exr-positive-matrices-b1.html: Let A=(211343314). Find the eigenvalues of A, its Perron root, Perron vector and left Perron vector. Check that no eigenvector for the other eigenvalues is non-negative.

exr-positive-matrices-b2.title: B2: Which order?
exr-positive-matrices-b2.html:
For each matrix, decide whether it is non-negative, whether it is positive, and whether it is positive definite. Justify your answers, and say whether @thm-perron applies.

  1. (2112)
  2. (1331)
  3. (2−1−12)
  4. (1023)
  5. (1111)

exr-positive-matrices-b3.title: B3: Bounds from the smallest and largest entry
exr-positive-matrices-b3.title_html: B3: Bounds from the smallest and largest entry
exr-positive-matrices-b3.html:
1. Show that ρ(cJ)=nc for every real c≥0, where J is the n×n all-ones matrix.
  2. Let A∈Mn(R) with a≤aij≤b for all i,j, where 0≤a≤b. Prove that na≤ρ(A)≤nb.
  3. Hence bound ρ(A) for A=(123231312), and compare with its exact value.

exr-positive-matrices-c1.title: C1: Symmetry passes to the Perron vector
exr-positive-matrices-c1.title_html: C1: Symmetry passes to the Perron vector
exr-positive-matrices-c1.html:
Let A>0 be n×n with Perron vector v, and let P be a permutation matrix with P⊤AP=A.

  1. Prove that Pv=v.
  2. Deduce that the Perron vector of A=(113113111) has equal first and second entries, and find it.
  3. Deduce that if A>0 commutes with the cyclic permutation matrix of 1→2→⋯→n→1, then its Perron vector is 1n1.

Hint: for (a), Pv is a positive vector in Δn.

exr-positive-matrices-c2.title: C2: Every conclusion fails for some non-negative matrix
exr-positive-matrices-c2.title_html: C2: Every conclusion fails for some non-negative matrix
exr-positive-matrices-c2.html: For each part of @thm-perron, (a) to (d), give a non-negative 2×2 matrix for which that part fails, and name the step of the proof that breaks. Then give a non-negative matrix for which (a), (b) and (c) fail at the same time.

exr-positive-matrices-c3.title: C3: The Perron root is strictly monotone
exr-positive-matrices-c3.title_html: C3: The Perron root is strictly monotone
exr-positive-matrices-c3.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(R) with 0<A≤B and A≠B.

  1. Prove that ρ(A)<ρ(B).
  2. Show by an example that the conclusion fails if A>0 is weakened to A≥0.

Hint: pair Bv with a positive left eigenvector of B, where v is the Perron vector of A.

exr-primitive-matrices-a1.title: A1
exr-primitive-matrices-a1.html:
1. Define a primitive matrix, and state the limit theorem for primitive matrices.
  2. True or false: every primitive matrix is irreducible. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: every irreducible non-negative matrix is primitive. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A≥0 is irreducible and a11>0, then A is primitive. Justify your answer.
  5. An irreducible A≥0 has ρ(A)=2 and period 4. Which of its eigenvalues can you name without further information?
  6. Name the two ingredients from earlier chapters that the proof of @thm-primitive-limit combines.

exr-primitive-matrices-b1.title: B1: Which are primitive?
exr-primitive-matrices-b1.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are primitive. Justify your answer.

  1. (0111).
  2. (010001100).
  3. (010101010).
  4. (110011001).

exr-primitive-matrices-b2.title: B2: A limit without diagonalizing
exr-primitive-matrices-b2.html:
Let A=(001201210).

  1. Show that A is primitive.
  2. Show that pA=(x−2)(x+1)2, and that A is not diagonalizable.
  3. Find positive right and left eigenvectors for ρ(A), and hence limm(A/2)m.

exr-primitive-matrices-b3.title: B3: Period and peripheral eigenvalues
exr-primitive-matrices-b3.html:
Let A=(010202010).

  1. Show that A is irreducible with period 2.
  2. Use @thm-peripheral-spectrum to predict the eigenvalues of modulus ρ(A) in terms of ρ(A), then compute pA and confirm.
  3. Hence explain why (A/ρ(A))m does not converge.

exr-primitive-matrices-c1.title: C1: Shifting by the identity
exr-primitive-matrices-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), A≥0, be irreducible, with right and left Perron vectors v,w, and let t>0.

  1. Prove that A+tI is primitive, with ρ(A+tI)=ρ(A)+t and the same Perron vectors v,w.
  2. Deduce that ((A+tI)/(ρ(A)+t))m→vw⊤/(w⊤v), and apply this to the swap with t=1.

exr-primitive-matrices-c2.title: C2: Traces detect the period
exr-primitive-matrices-c2.html:
Let A≥0 be irreducible, not the 1×1 zero matrix, with period h.

  1. Prove that tr(Am)=0 for every m≥1 that is not a multiple of h, in two ways: from @thm-peripheral-spectrum (b), and from @lem-powers-and-walks (a).
  2. Deduce that if tr(A2)>0 and tr(A3)>0, then A is primitive.
  3. Check (b) on the matrix W of the examples.

exr-primitive-matrices-c3.title: C3: A finite test for primitivity
exr-primitive-matrices-c3.title_html: C3: A finite test for primitivity
exr-primitive-matrices-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), A≥0, and let Zm be the zero pattern of Am: the 0/1 matrix with a 1 exactly where Am is positive.

  1. Prove that Zm+1 is determined by Zm and Z1.
  2. Deduce that if Za=Zb with a<b, then Za+j=Zb+j for every j≥0.
  3. Prove that if A is primitive, then Ak>0 for some k≤2n2. Compare with @thm-wielandt-bound.

Hint: there are only 2n2 zero patterns; use @prp-primitive-basic (a).

lem-absorbing-transient-decay.title: Transient Mass Dies Out
lem-absorbing-transient-decay.html: If A is absorbing, with Q as above, then every eigenvalue of Q has modulus less than 1, and Qm→0.

lem-diagonal-doubly-stochastic-image.title: The Diagonal Is a Doubly Stochastic Image of the Spectrum
lem-diagonal-doubly-stochastic-image.title_html: The Diagonal Is a Doubly Stochastic Image of the Spectrum
lem-diagonal-doubly-stochastic-image.html: Let F=R or C, let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, and let A=UDU∗ with U unitary and D=diag(λ1(A),…,λn(A)). Then the matrix S=(|uij|2) is doubly stochastic, and 𝛌d(A)=Sλ(A). Such a U exists by @cor-spectral-complex-matrix, after reordering the columns of U, since a Hermitian matrix is normal: the diagonal entries of the D it gives are the eigenvalues of A with multiplicity, because similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial pA (@thm-charpoly-similarity-invariant), and they are real (@thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues), so they can be put in decreasing order.

lem-doubly-stochastic-sum-conditions.title: The Row and Column Sum Conditions
lem-doubly-stochastic-sum-conditions.title_html: The Row and Column Sum Conditions
lem-doubly-stochastic-sum-conditions.html:
Let n≥1, and let Wn={X∈Mn(R):X1=0, 1⊤X=0⊤} be the space of real matrices whose rows and columns all add up to 0. Then:

  1. dim⁡Wn=(n−1)2;
  2. the 2n matrices R1,…,Rn,C1,…,Cn span a subspace of Mn(R) of dimension 2n−1.

lem-entrywise-absolute-value.title: Absolute Value of a Product
lem-entrywise-absolute-value.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(C), B∈Mn×p(C) and x∈Cn. Then

  1. |Ax|≤|A||x|;
  2. |AB|≤|A||B|;
  3. if m=n, then |Ak|≤|A|k for every k≥0.

lem-entrywise-order-rules.title: Rules of the Entrywise Order
lem-entrywise-order-rules.html:
Let A,B∈Mm×n(R), C,D∈Mn×p(R) and x,y∈Rn.

  1. If 0≤A≤B and 0≤x≤y, then 0≤Ax≤By.
  2. If A>0, x≥0 and x≠0, then Ax>0.
  3. If 0≤A≤B and 0≤C≤D, then 0≤AC≤BD. In particular, for square 0≤A≤B, 0≤Ak≤Bk for every k≥0.

lem-permutation-similarity-entries.title: Relabeling the Coordinates
lem-permutation-similarity-entries.html: Let σ∈Sn and A∈Mn(F). Then (Pσ⊤APσ)st=aσ(s)σ(t) for all s,t. Consequently t→s is an edge of G(Pσ⊤APσ) if and only if σ(t)→σ(s) is an edge of G(A).

lem-powers-and-walks.title: Powers Count Walks
lem-powers-and-walks.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be non-negative, and let k≥0 and i,j∈{1,…,n}.

  1. (Ak)ij>0 if and only if G(A) has a walk of length k from j to i.
  2. ((I+A)k)ij>0 if and only if G(A) has a walk of length at most k from j to i.

lem-reducible-closed-set.title: Reducible Means a Set of Vertices With No Exit
lem-reducible-closed-set.title_html: Reducible Means a Set of Vertices With No Exit
lem-reducible-closed-set.html: Let n≥2 and A∈Mn(F). Then A is reducible if and only if there is a set S⊆{1,…,n} with S≠∅ and S≠{1,…,n} such that aij=0whenever j∈S and i∉S, that is, such that no edge of G(A) goes from a vertex in S to a vertex outside S.

lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix.title: The Smallest Real Eigenvalue of a Z-Matrix
lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix.title_html: The Smallest Real Eigenvalue of a Z-Matrix
lem-smallest-real-eigenvalue-z-matrix.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be a Z-matrix, and let A=sI−B with B≥0 be any representation as in @lem-z-matrix-as-shift.

  1. s−ρ(B) is an eigenvalue of A, and every λ∈spec(A) satisfies Reλ≥s−ρ(B). In particular s−ρ(B) is the smallest real eigenvalue of A, and so it is the same number for every representation.
  2. A is an M-matrix if and only if s≥ρ(B), and a non-singular M-matrix if and only if s>ρ(B).

lem-test-vector-principal-submatrix.title: Test Vectors Survive Deletion
lem-test-vector-principal-submatrix.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be a Z-matrix, and let x∈Rn satisfy x>0 and Ax>0. Let S⊆[n] be non-empty, let AS,S be the principal submatrix on rows and columns S (@def-submatrix-minor), and let xS be the vector of the entries xj, j∈S, in increasing order of j. Then AS,S is a Z-matrix, xS>0 and AS,SxS>0.

lem-triangle-equality-complex.title: Equality in the Triangle Inequality
lem-triangle-equality-complex.html: Let z1,…,zm∈C, put s=z1+⋯+zm, and suppose |s|=|z1|+⋯+|zm| and s≠0. Then zj=|zj|c for every j, where c=s/|s| has |c|=1.

lem-walk-contains-path.title: Shortening a Walk to a Path
lem-walk-contains-path.title_html: Shortening a Walk to a Path
lem-walk-contains-path.html: Let A∈Mn(F). If G(A) has a walk from j to i, then it has a path from j to i, and every path has length at most n−1.

lem-z-matrix-as-shift.title: Z-Matrices Are Shifts of Non-negative Matrices
lem-z-matrix-as-shift.title_html: Z-Matrices Are Shifts of Non-negative Matrices
lem-z-matrix-as-shift.html: A matrix A∈Mn(R) is a Z-matrix if and only if A=sI−B for some real s and some B∈Mn(R) with B≥0. For a Z-matrix, every s≥maxiaii gives such a representation, with B=sI−A.

prp-doubly-stochastic-image-majorized.title: Doubly Stochastic Maps Even Out
prp-doubly-stochastic-image-majorized.html: Let S∈Ωn and y∈Rn. Then Sy≺y.

prp-pagerank-contraction.title: Convergence at the Damping Rate
prp-pagerank-contraction.html: Let P, α, G and 𝛑π be as in @thm-pagerank-vector, let x0 be any probability vector, and let xk=Gkx0. Then for every k≥0, 𝛑𝛑‖xk−π‖1≤αk‖x0−π‖1≤2αk. In particular, 𝛑xk→π entrywise.

prp-primitive-basic.title: First Properties of Primitive Matrices
prp-primitive-basic.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be primitive, with Ak>0. Then:

  1. Am>0 for every m≥k;
  2. A is irreducible;
  3. ρ(A)>0, and ρ(A) is the only eigenvalue of A of modulus ρ(A).

prp-second-difference-inverse.title: The Second-Difference Matrix
prp-second-difference-inverse.html: Let n≥1. Then Kn is a non-singular M-matrix, and its inverse is the matrix with entries (Kn−1)ij=min(i,j)(n+1−max(i,j))n+1,1≤i,j≤n. In particular every entry of Kn−1 is positive.

prp-spectral-radius-monotone.title: Monotonicity of the Spectral Radius
prp-spectral-radius-monotone.html:
1. If A,B∈Mn(R) and 0≤A≤B, then ρ(A)≤ρ(B).
  2. More generally, if A∈Mn(C), B∈Mn(R) and |A|≤B, then ρ(A)≤ρ(|A|)≤ρ(B).

prp-stochastic-perron.title: The Perron Root of a Stochastic Matrix
prp-stochastic-perron.title_html: The Perron Root of a Stochastic Matrix
prp-stochastic-perron.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic. Then:

  1. ρ(A)=1, and 1 is a positive left eigenvector for it;
  2. the steady states of A are exactly the non-negative eigenvectors for ρ(A) whose entries sum to 1;
  3. if A is irreducible, then A has exactly one steady state v, and v>0.

prp-subinvariance.title: Subinvariance
prp-subinvariance.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) with A≥0, and let s∈R.

  1. If x>0 and Ax≤sx, then ρ(A)≤s.
  2. If A is irreducible, x≥0, x≠0 and Ax≤sx, then ρ(A)≤s. If moreover Ax≠sx, then ρ(A)<s.

prp-superinvariance.title: Superinvariance
prp-superinvariance.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) with A≥0, let s∈R, and let x≥0, x≠0, with Ax≥sx.

  1. Then ρ(A)≥s.
  2. If A is irreducible and Ax≠sx, then ρ(A)>s.

thm-absorbing-chain.title: Absorbing Chains
thm-absorbing-chain.html:
Let A=(Q0RIr) be absorbing, in the block form above. Then:

  1. I−Q is invertible, and the fundamental matrix N:=(I−Q)−1=∑k≥0Qk satisfies N≥0;
  2. Am→(00RNIr) entrywise;
  3. every column of the r×t matrix B:=RN is a probability vector.

thm-birkhoff.title: Birkhoff’s Theorem
thm-birkhoff.html: Let n≥1. The extreme points of Ωn are exactly the n! permutation matrices of size n. Equivalently, every doubly stochastic matrix is a convex combination of permutation matrices: Ωn=conv{Pσ:σ∈Sn}.

thm-collatz-wielandt.title: Collatz–Wielandt Formula
thm-collatz-wielandt.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be non-negative and irreducible, with Perron vector v (@def-perron-root-and-vectors). Then ρ(A)=maxx≥0x≠0r―A(x)=minx>0r―A(x), both extreme values are attained at x=v, and they are attained only at the positive multiples of v: if x≥0, x≠0 and r―A(x)=ρ(A), or if x>0 and r―A(x)=ρ(A), then x is a positive multiple of v.

thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues.title: The Eigenvalues of the Google Matrix
thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues.title_html: The Eigenvalues of the Google Matrix
thm-google-matrix-eigenvalues.html: Let n≥2, let P∈Mn(R) be stochastic, let 0≤α≤1, and let G=αP+1−αnJ. Since 1 is an eigenvalue of P (@prp-stochastic-properties) and pP splits over C (@thm-fundamental-theorem-of-algebra), it factors as pP(x)=(x−1)(x−μ2)⋯(x−μn) with μ2,…,μn∈C. Then pG(x)=(x−1)(x−αμ2)⋯(x−αμn). In particular, if α<1, every eigenvalue λ≠1 of G satisfies |λ|≤α.

thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected.title: Irreducible If and Only If Strongly Connected
thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected.title_html: Irreducible If and Only If Strongly Connected
thm-irreducible-iff-strongly-connected.html: Let n≥1 and A∈Mn(F). Then A is irreducible if and only if G(A) is strongly connected.

thm-irreducible-power-positive.title: Irreducibility Through a Power of \I + \A
thm-irreducible-power-positive.title_html: Irreducibility Through a Power of I+A
thm-irreducible-power-positive.html: Let n≥1 and let A∈Mn(R) be non-negative. Then A is irreducible if and only if (I+A)n−1>0.

thm-m-matrix-characterizations.title: Characterizations of Non-singular M-Matrices
thm-m-matrix-characterizations.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), n≥1, be a Z-matrix. The following are equivalent.

  1. A is a non-singular M-matrix.
  2. A is invertible and A−1≥0.
  3. There is x∈Rn with x>0 and Ax>0.
  4. Every eigenvalue of A in C has positive real part.
  5. Every real eigenvalue of A is positive.
  6. Every principal minor of A is positive: detAS,S>0 for every non-empty S⊆[n].
  7. Every leading principal minor of A is positive: detAk>0 for k=1,…,n.

thm-markov-cesaro.title: Averages of an Irreducible Chain
thm-markov-cesaro.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic and irreducible, with steady state v. Then:

  1. 1m(I+A+A2+⋯+Am−1)→v1⊤ as m→∞;
  2. for every probability vector x0, the averages 1m(x0+x1+⋯+xm−1) of the chain converge to v;
  3. Am converges if and only if A is primitive.

thm-markov-limit-primitive.title: Long-Run Behavior of a Markov Chain
thm-markov-limit-primitive.title_html: Long-Run Behavior of a Markov Chain
thm-markov-limit-primitive.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be stochastic, and suppose that Ak>0 for some k≥1. Then:

  1. A has exactly one steady state v, and v>0;
  2. Am→v1⊤ entrywise as m→∞;
  3. for every probability vector x0, the Markov chain xm=Amx0 converges entrywise to v.

thm-nonnegative-rho-eigenvalue.title: The Spectral Radius of a Non-negative Matrix Is an Eigenvalue
thm-nonnegative-rho-eigenvalue.title_html: The Spectral Radius of a Non-negative Matrix Is an Eigenvalue
thm-nonnegative-rho-eigenvalue.html: Let A∈Mn(R) with n≥1 and A≥0. Then ρ(A) is an eigenvalue of A, and there is a vector x∈Rn with x≥0, x≠0 and Ax=ρ(A)x.

thm-pagerank-vector.title: The PageRank Vector
thm-pagerank-vector.html:
Let P∈Mn(R) be stochastic, 0<α<1, and G=αP+1−αnJ. Then:

  1. ρ(G)=1, and 1 is an eigenvalue of G of algebraic multiplicity one;
  2. there is exactly one probability vector 𝛑π with 𝛑𝛑Gπ=π, and every entry of 𝛑π is positive;
  3. I−αP is invertible, and 𝛑π is the unique solution of 𝛑(I−αP)π=1−αn1.

thm-peripheral-spectrum.title: The Peripheral Spectrum
thm-peripheral-spectrum.html:
Let A∈Mn(R), A≥0, be irreducible and not the 1×1 zero matrix. Put ρ=ρ(A), let h be the number of distinct eigenvalues of A of modulus ρ, and let ω=e2πi/h. Then:

  1. the eigenvalues of A of modulus ρ are exactly ρ,ρω,ρω2,…,ρωh−1, and each is algebraically simple;
  2. A is similar to ωA; in particular spec(A) is unchanged by multiplication by ω, with algebraic multiplicities;
  3. h equals the period of A.

thm-perron.title: Perron’s Theorem
thm-perron.html:
Let n≥1 and let A∈Mn(R) be positive, A>0. Write r=ρ(A). Then:

  1. r>0, and r is an eigenvalue of A with an eigenvector v>0;
  2. r is algebraically simple: aA(r)=1. In particular Er(A)=span(v);
  3. every eigenvalue λ∈C of A with λ≠r satisfies |λ|<r;
  4. every non-negative eigenvector of A is a positive multiple of v. In particular, no eigenvector of A for an eigenvalue other than r is non-negative;
  5. A⊤ is positive with ρ(A⊤)=r, so (a)–(d) hold for A⊤: there is w>0 with w⊤A=rw⊤.

thm-perron-frobenius.title: Perron–Frobenius Theorem
thm-perron-frobenius.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) with n≥1 be non-negative and irreducible, and put ρ=ρ(A). Then:

  1. ρ is an eigenvalue of A with an eigenvector v>0;
  2. ρ is algebraically simple: aA(ρ)=1;
  3. every non-negative eigenvector of A, for any eigenvalue, is a positive multiple of v; in particular its eigenvalue is ρ, and the non-negative eigenvector is unique up to scale;
  4. if n≥2, then ρ>0.

thm-primitive-iff-single-peripheral.title: Primitivity from the Spectrum
thm-primitive-iff-single-peripheral.html: Let A∈Mn(R), A≥0, be irreducible with ρ(A)>0. Then A is primitive if and only if ρ(A) is the only eigenvalue of A of modulus ρ(A).

thm-primitive-limit.title: Limit Theorem for Primitive Matrices
thm-primitive-limit.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be primitive, ρ=ρ(A), and let v>0 and w>0 satisfy Av=ρv and w⊤A=ρw⊤, for instance the right and left Perron vectors of A. Then, entrywise, (1ρA)m⟶vw⊤w⊤v(m→∞). The limit is a positive matrix of rank one, and it does not depend on how v and w are scaled. The same conclusion holds for every irreducible A≥0 with ρ(A)>0 whose only eigenvalue of modulus ρ(A) is ρ(A) itself.

thm-reducible-normal-form.title: Reducible Normal Form
thm-reducible-normal-form.html:
Let n≥1 and A∈Mn(F).

  1. There are a permutation matrix P and an integer m≥1 such that P⊤AP=(A11A12⋯A1m0A22⋯A2m⋮⋱⋮0⋯0Amm), block upper triangular, with every diagonal block Aii square and irreducible.
  2. In that case pA=pA11pA22⋯pAmm, so the eigenvalues of A, with their algebraic multiplicities, are those of the diagonal blocks taken together.
  3. ρ(A)=maxiρ(Aii); if A≥0, every Aii≥0.

thm-wielandt-bound.title: Wielandt’s Bound
thm-wielandt-bound.html: If A∈Mn(R) is primitive, then A(n−1)2+1>0. The bound cannot be improved: for n≥2 the matrix Wn with ones at the positions (i,i+1) for i<n and at (n,1) and (n,2), and zeros elsewhere, is primitive and Wn(n−1)2 has a zero entry.
